title: First exchange
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A yes/no question is the statement, unchanged, said with a rising voice and written with a question mark: Sei di Roma? beside Sei di Roma. Nothing moves to the front, and there is no Italian word doing the job of English "do".
Wellbeing runs on stare, not on essere: Come stai? · Sto bene. essere says who or what you are (M1); stare says how you are doing.
An adjective agrees with the SUBJECT — with whoever or whatever the sentence is about: sono stanco (a man about himself) · sono stanca (a woman) · sei stanca? (asked of a woman).

Three words for opening and closing, and each has its own job: ciao is for someone you are on familiar terms with and does both hello and goodbye; buongiorno is the daytime greeting you can say to anyone; arrivederci is the neutral goodbye.
The accent on sì is a letter, not emphasis. sì is "yes"; si without it is the little pronoun of si chiama, a different word entirely.

This course speaks to one person as tu, so every "you" verb ends in -i: sei, stai, ti chiami. Italian also has a polite address, Lei, which takes the he/she form of the verb (Come sta?); it belongs to a later level and is not used here.
essere carries on doing what M1 taught, one shape per person: sono (I) · sei (you) · è (he, she, it).

sentences.glossEn: "Hi, Anna" — ciao does hello and goodbye alike

words.note: One word for both ends of a conversation — hello on the way in, goodbye on the way out. It is warm rather than neutral: it belongs with people you are on tu terms with.
Names carry over unchanged — swap in the name of whoever you are talking to.

sentences.trap: ciao is not the neutral greeting English speakers expect it to be. To a stranger, a shopkeeper or someone much older, buongiorno is the safer word.
sentences.sound: CHOW. The c before i is the ch of "church", and -iao runs together as one syllable.

variations.changed: swap the name — Ciao itself never changes
the same word on the way out — ciao closes a conversation as well as opening one
the daytime greeting instead, for when ciao would be too familiar

mistake.why: Pick one. ciao and buongiorno both open a conversation, and stacking them is not politer — only strange.

sentences.usage: Meeting a friend, and leaving one.
sentences.mnemonic: ciao arrives and leaves by the same door.

sentences.glossEn: "Good morning, Rohan" — one word, buon + giorno

words.note: "Good day", written as one word. It covers the morning and the early part of the afternoon, not just the hour after breakfast, and it is the greeting that works with anyone — a friend, a stranger, a shopkeeper.

sentences.trap: English splits "good morning" in two and keeps it to the morning. Italian welds it into one word and runs it through the middle of the day.
sentences.sound: bwon-JOR-no. The gi is the j of "jam", one sound and not two.

variations.changed: swap the name — the greeting is the frame
no name at all — walking into a shop, this is the whole greeting
the familiar greeting instead, for someone you know well

mistake.why: come sta? is the polite address, Lei, which this course does not teach. Speaking to one person as tu it is come stai? — and buongiorno works with either.

sentences.usage: Any daytime greeting where ciao would be too familiar — a shop, an office, a stranger.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "How are you doing?" — the verb is stare, not essere

words.note: how — the question word, and it stands at the front exactly as in English.
stare, the verb of how things are GOING, as against essere for what they ARE. The ending names the person: sto (I) · stai (you). It is the verb every enquiry after someone's health uses.

sentences.trap: There is no "are" to add and no "do" to front. Come stai? is the whole question, and the rising voice — with the question mark that writes it — is all that marks it as one.
sentences.sound: KO-me STAI. stai is one syllable: the a and the i glide together, close to the English word "sty".

variations.changed: a name after the question, exactly where English puts one
the same verb as a yes/no question — nothing moves, only the voice rises
the answer: the same verb, with the io ending

mistake.why: essere asks what you ARE — tall, Italian, a student. How you are doing takes stare: Come stai?

sentences.usage: The second thing you say, after the greeting.
sentences.mnemonic: stare is how you are standing today; essere is who you are.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Am doing well, thanks" — the "I" is inside sto

words.note: well — an adverb, and it answers a verb. English answers "how are you?" with an adjective (I'm fine, I'm good); Italian answers with this. buono is the adjective and describes a thing, not how someone is doing.
thank you — one word for the whole phrase, and it never changes shape.

sentences.trap: English reaches for an adjective here — I'm good. Italian will not: how you are doing is bene, and Sto buono, if it says anything, says you are behaving yourself.
sentences.sound: BEH-ne, then GRAH-tsye. That z is a "ts" again, exactly as in canzoni.

variations.changed: molto in front of bene turns it up
sto → stai: the same answer turned into a question about you
a name on the end, where English also puts one

mistake.why: buono is an adjective and describes a thing (il caffè è buono); with stare it is about behaving yourself, not about your health. How you are doing takes the adverb: Sto bene.

sentences.usage: The standard answer, whether or not it is the whole truth.
sentences.mnemonic: bene answers a verb; buono describes a thing.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Are from Rome?" — the "you" is inside sei

words.note: essere for tu, the one person this course speaks to: sono (I) · sei (you) · è (he, she, it). Italian spells the number six the same way — sei — and only the sentence around it tells you which one you are looking at.
City names carry over, though Italian spells its own: Roma, not Rome.

sentences.trap: English has to move something to ask — are you, do you. Italian moves nothing at all: the question is the statement with a rising voice, and *Fai sei di Roma? is an auxiliary Italian has no use for.
sentences.sound: SEY, one syllable, and RO-ma with an open o and a tapped r.

variations.changed: swap the city — Sei di …? is the frame
the same four words as a statement — only the question mark, and the voice, has gone
swap what is being asked about — and after essere the role is still bare

mistake.why: Drop the tu — sei already says "you are". Keep it only to single someone out from other people.

sentences.usage: Asking where someone is from, once you are past the greeting.
sentences.mnemonic: The -i ending is the "you": sei, stai, ti chiami.

sentences.glossEn: "Yes, am from Rome" — the answer repeats the verb, not the pronoun

words.note: yes. The accent is part of the word, not emphasis: si without it is the little pronoun of si chiama, and the two are otherwise identical on the page.

sentences.trap: English answers with the auxiliary — Yes, I am. Italian has no auxiliary to reach for, so it either says sì alone or says sì and then the whole short sentence.
sentences.sound: SEE, held a beat, and the accent is telling you it carries the stress of the word all on its own.

variations.changed: swap the city; the answer's shape holds
the same yes in front of a different statement
on its own — a complete answer, with no verb behind it

mistake.why: Without its accent si is a different word — the pronoun in si chiama. "Yes" is sì, every time.

sentences.usage: Agreeing, and then saying the thing you are agreeing to.
sentences.mnemonic: sì leans on its accent the way è does.

sentences.glossEn: "No, am from Delhi" — the correction follows the no

words.note: no — the same little word as in English, with no accent on it and nothing else to remember.

sentences.trap: English softens a correction with an auxiliary — no, I'm not, I'm from Delhi. Italian puts no in front and then simply says the true sentence.
sentences.sound: NAW, with an open o held cleanly — Italian never lets it slide into the "oh" of English "no".

variations.changed: swap the city that is true
the other everyday no — a refusal, softened by grazie
on its own — a complete answer

mistake.why: no carries no accent. The accented words of this module are sì and è; no is not one of them.

sentences.usage: Correcting a guess about you, politely and in one breath.
sentences.mnemonic: no is bare; sì wears an accent.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Are tired?" — asked of a man

words.note: tired, and it agrees with whoever the sentence is about: stanco of a man, stanca of a woman, stanchi and stanche in the plural. The h in stanchi and stanche is doing no work of its own — it keeps the c hard, as it does in amiche.

sentences.trap: English "tired" never changes, so the ending here is easy to leave on the default. It follows the SUBJECT, not the speaker: asked of a woman it is Sei stanca?, whoever is doing the asking.
sentences.sound: STAN-ko. The c before o is a hard k; the same c before i or e would be the ch of "church", which is why stanchi needs its h.

variations.changed: -o → -a: the same question asked of a woman
sei → sono: the answer, in the first person
a name as the subject, and è as the verb that goes with it

mistake.why: Anna is a woman, so the adjective has to move with her: Anna, sei stanca? The ending answers to the subject, never to whoever is speaking.

sentences.usage: Checking on someone at the end of a long day.
sentences.mnemonic: The adjective follows the person it is about, like a shadow.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Am tired today" — said by a woman

words.note: today. A time word can stand at the end, as here, or at the front (Oggi sono stanca) — Italian is content either way.

sentences.trap: The -a is not a typo and not a softening: it is there because the person speaking is a woman. A man saying the same thing writes Sono stanco.
sentences.sound: OD-ji, two syllables, and the double g is held — Italian doubles consonants audibly, and the gg before i is the j of "jam".

variations.changed: -a → -o: the same sentence said by a man
the time word moved to the front — nothing else has to move with it
sono → sei and a question mark: the same words asked instead of stated

mistake.why: Drop the io — sono already says "I am". It comes back only to draw a contrast with somebody else.

sentences.usage: Explaining yourself, or turning down an invitation gently.
sentences.mnemonic: oggi has two g's because today is heavy.

sentences.glossEn: "Goodbye, Rohan" — the neutral goodbye, for anyone

words.note: goodbye, and it works with anyone — where ciao would be too familiar, this is the word. It is built out of "until we see each other again", which is why it is so long.

sentences.trap: English has one "goodbye" for every situation. Italian splits the job: ciao to a friend, arrivederci to everyone else — and using ciao where arrivederci belongs is the same over-familiarity as using ciao to open.
sentences.sound: ar-ri-ve-DER-chi. The double r is trilled longer than a single one, and the final -ci is "chee".

variations.changed: swap the name — the goodbye is the frame
no name — leaving a shop, this is the whole line
the familiar goodbye instead, for someone you know well

mistake.why: buongiorno opens; arrivederci closes. Putting them together says hello and goodbye in the same breath.

sentences.usage: Leaving a shop, an office, or any conversation with someone you are not on ciao terms with.
sentences.mnemonic: arrivederci is long because it means "until we see each other again".
